title: Lines and Angles
prerequisites: Knowledge of types of angles — acute, right, obtuse, straight.
Ability to measure an angle with a protractor.
Idea of parallel and intersecting lines.
Understanding that angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

topics.title: Pairs of Angles and Intersecting Lines
topics.quick_summary: Angles formed at a point or on a line follow fixed relationships — linear pairs sum to 180° and vertically opposite angles are always equal.
topics.real_life: Two crossing roads always create equal angles opposite each other, which is why a junction looks symmetric from opposite corners.

detailed.definition: Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary angles sum to 180°. A linear pair is a pair of adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line. Vertically opposite angles are the pairs of opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines.
detailed.key_idea: Vertically opposite angles are equal because each is supplementary to the same adjacent angle. The proof is one line, and it is a standard two-mark question.
detailed.working_principle: The sum of all angles at a point is 360°, and the sum of angles on one side of a straight line is 180°. Every angle-chasing problem reduces to repeated use of these two facts.
applications: Adjacent angles share a common vertex and a common arm but no common interior points.
If two lines intersect, both pairs of vertically opposite angles are equal.
Angles around a point add to 360°.

points: A linear pair is always supplementary.
Vertically opposite angles are always equal.
Angles at a point sum to 360°.
Two supplementary adjacent angles form a linear pair, so their outer arms are collinear.
mistakes: Assuming any two equal angles are vertically opposite; they must be formed by two intersecting lines.
Treating adjacent angles as necessarily forming a linear pair.
topics.memory_hook: 'C comes before S, and 90 comes before 180' — Complementary 90, Supplementary 180.
topics.advanced: The linear pair axiom and its converse together are equivalent to the statement that a straight angle measures exactly 180°. Much of elementary geometry rests on this single normalisation.

topics.title: Parallel Lines and a Transversal
topics.quick_summary: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles are supplementary.
topics.real_life: Railway sleepers cut across two parallel rails at the same angle every time — that constancy is exactly the corresponding-angles property.

detailed.definition: A transversal is a line that intersects two or more lines at distinct points. It creates corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior and co-interior (allied) angle pairs.
detailed.key_idea: Each of these three properties is both a test for parallelism and a consequence of it. Given parallel lines you may use the equalities; given the equalities you may conclude the lines are parallel.
detailed.working_principle: In angle chasing, mark all equal angles first using corresponding and alternate pairs, then use the linear pair and angle-sum facts to fill in the rest.
applications: Corresponding angles equal ⟺ lines are parallel.
Alternate interior angles equal ⟺ lines are parallel.
Co-interior angles supplementary ⟺ lines are parallel.

points: Corresponding angles: equal when the lines are parallel (F-shape).
Alternate interior angles: equal when the lines are parallel (Z-shape).
Co-interior (allied) angles: supplementary when the lines are parallel (C or U-shape).
Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other.
Each property works in both directions — as a consequence and as a test.
mistakes: Saying co-interior angles are equal; they are supplementary.
Applying these properties when the lines are not known to be parallel.
Mixing up alternate interior with alternate exterior angles.
topics.memory_hook: 'F for corresponding, Z for alternate, C for co-interior' — and only C adds to 180°.
topics.advanced: All three properties depend on Euclid's fifth postulate. On a sphere, where 'lines' are great circles, no two lines are parallel at all and none of these results holds.

topics.title: Angle Sum Property of a Triangle
topics.quick_summary: The three angles of a triangle always add to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
topics.real_life: A surveyor checks measurements by confirming that the three measured angles of a triangular plot total 180° — any excess signals an error.

detailed.definition: The angle sum property states that the sum of the three interior angles of a triangle is 180°. The exterior angle property states that an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
detailed.key_idea: The exterior angle property follows immediately from the angle sum property together with the linear pair at that vertex, so the second result is really a corollary of the first.
detailed.working_principle: The angle sum is proved by drawing a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and using alternate angles. This is the standard proof expected in the examination.
applications: A triangle can have at most one right angle or one obtuse angle.
In an equilateral triangle each angle is 60°.
The exterior angle is always greater than either interior opposite angle.

points: Sum of the interior angles of a triangle = 180°.
Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles.
A triangle cannot have two right angles or two obtuse angles.
The angle sum property is proved using a parallel line through one vertex.
Sum of the exterior angles of any polygon, taken one at each vertex, is 360°.
mistakes: Adding the exterior angle to all three interior angles.
Assuming the exterior angle equals the adjacent interior angle.
Forgetting that the property holds only in plane (Euclidean) geometry.
topics.memory_hook: 'Three angles, one straight line — 180° every time.'
topics.advanced: On a sphere the angles of a triangle sum to more than 180°, and the excess is proportional to its area. Gauss reportedly tried to measure this excess on mountain triangles to test whether physical space is Euclidean.
